case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Louisiana’s COVID-era Health Emergency Powers Act immunity (requiring gross negligence or willful misconduct) may be applied in state court to defeat or heighten the liability standard for federal disability-discrimination claims under the ADA and the Rehabilitation Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Louisiana Health Emergency Powers Act (LHEPA) immunity provisions (as applied during the declared COVID-19 public health emergency) in relation to Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (and the Supremacy Clause/preemption principles implicated by that interaction).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that his suit is not a state tort/malpractice action but a federal civil-rights action under the ADA and Rehabilitation Act, and Louisiana courts improperly imported LHEPA’s heightened culpability requirement (gross negligence/willful misconduct) into the elements of those federal causes of action. He contends this state-law immunity regime, as applied, obstructs Congress’s national mandate against disability discrimination, undermines uniform enforcement of federal rights, and should be preempted under the Supremacy Clause. He also argues the Louisiana Supreme Court’s writ denial (and the First Circuit’s decision) rested on state immunity rather than addressing the merits of the federal discrimination claims, creating a dangerous precedent that emergencies can condition or suspend federal civil-rights protections.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue the petition rests on an incorrect premise about remedies and viability of the federal claims: compensatory emotional-distress damages are not available under Title III of the ADA in a private enforcement action, and are likewise unavailable under § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act per Supreme Court precedent (Cummings). They maintain that, independent of LHEPA, petitioner cannot obtain the damages he seeks. They also defend the Louisiana courts’ use of LHEPA during the COVID emergency as a permissible state-law limitation on civil liability for healthcare providers (except for gross negligence or willful misconduct), and contend the petition does not adequately establish preemption (including that petitioner offered only conclusory assertions without authority).
key_precedents: Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. (2022) (emotional distress damages unavailable under Spending Clause statutes such as § 504)
Mills v. Hartford Healthcare Corp., 347 A.3d 605 (Conn. 2023) (example of state-court interpretation of COVID-era immunity provisions)
Resurgens, LLC v. Ervin, 894 S.E.2d 408 (Ga. 2023) (example of state-court interpretation of COVID-era immunity provisions)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest point that, under Howlett and Haywood, a State generally cannot graft a heightened culpability standard onto the merits of a federal cause of action, even when the principal relief is injunctive or fees. But those precedents assume a demonstrated displacement of an operative federal entitlement, and here (as Justice Alito and Justice Barrett stress) petitioner has not shown on this record that LHEPA actually foreclosed any federally authorized relief—Title III private suits are largely injunctive and Cummings substantially undercuts the pleaded § 504 damages theory—making a Supremacy Clause ruling both broad and potentially advisory. Minimalism and institutional legitimacy counsel resolving the case on the antecedent remedial/vehicle ground and leaving the Howlett/Haywood preemption question for a cleaner case where a viable federal remedy is plainly denied solely because a state immunity overlay was applied. I therefore remain with respondent.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor’s Howlett/Haywood point is the strongest pushback: a State may not interpose a state-law “immunity” or heightened culpability rule to alter the elements of a federal claim. But those cases presuppose that a federal right with an operative, congressionally authorized avenue of relief is actually being displaced; as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito emphasize, on this record petitioner’s pleaded theory is largely remedially unavailable under the federal statutes themselves (Title III’s limits and Cummings’s bar on emotional-distress damages), making any Supremacy Clause conflict with LHEPA too indeterminate and close to advisory. As a textualist/originalist, I will not infer preemption of a generally applicable state emergency-liability rule absent a concrete, outcome-determinative clash with specific federal relief Congress provided as applied here, including prospective relief and fees. I would therefore affirm on the narrow vehicle/remedy ground and reserve the Howlett question for a case where the state rule demonstrably forecloses federally authorized relief.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s “preempt only as to merits” proposal is the strongest push on the other side, and I accept her premise (echoed by Justice Sotomayor) that Howlett and Haywood forbid a State from substantively rewriting the elements of a federal cause of action via a state-law immunity. But those cases presuppose that the state rule actually displaces an operative federal entitlement, and here—per the Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s remedial-threshold point—petitioner has not shown that LHEPA foreclosed any relief Congress actually made available on this record: Title III private relief is largely injunctive and Cummings undercuts the central § 504 emotional-distress damages theory. Justice Gorsuch is right that prospective relief and fees can matter, but the record does not clearly establish that LHEPA was outcome-determinative as to any such federal remedy rather than simply academic given the pleaded remedial theory. Without a concrete, as-applied conflict that changes the available federal relief, a Supremacy Clause holding would be unnecessarily broad and too close to advisory; I would reserve Howlett/Haywood for a cleaner vehicle where a viable federal remedy is plainly denied solely because of the state overlay.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s remedial-threshold argument is the strongest pushback, but it wrongly treats remedial limits as eliminating the federal entitlement itself; even where damages are narrowed by Title III and Cummings, federal law still creates enforceable duties and authorizes at least prospective relief and fees, and Louisiana cannot transform that merits inquiry into a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct screen. Howlett v. Rose and Haywood v. Drown apply precisely when a State uses a purported “immunity” to alter the elements of a federal claim, and that conflict exists independent of whether the plaintiff ultimately recovers compensatory damages. Justice Kagan’s narrow disposition answers the institutional-legitimacy concern: hold LHEPA preempted only to the extent it was used as a merits-stage gatekeeper for ADA/§ 504 liability, while leaving all remedy questions (including Cummings and Title III limits) for remand. Accepting respondents’ framing would predictably under-enforce disability protections for vulnerable patients in emergencies by letting States extinguish federal liability through culpability overlays Congress did not enact.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s remedial-threshold point seriously, but it treats “limited remedies” as if it meant “no federally enforceable right,” and Howlett and Haywood reject that move when a State uses its own law to alter the merits elements Congress set. Even if Title III is chiefly injunctive and Cummings narrows § 504 damages, those remedial limits are Congress’s choice; Louisiana cannot convert the federal nondiscrimination/reasonable-modification duty into a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct regime as a merits gatekeeper, which predictably also forecloses prospective relief and fees. Justice Kavanaugh is right to caution against an unnecessary Supremacy Clause holding, but we can be narrow and pragmatic: preempt LHEPA only to the extent it was applied to change the ADA/§ 504 liability standard, and remand for the lower courts to sort out which remedies (if any) remain available under Title III and Cummings. Justice Sotomayor’s framing underscores why this is not advisory—state-law “immunities” cannot be used to rewrite federal duties in state court, even when the ultimate relief may be constrained.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s (and Justice Kavanaugh’s) remedial-threshold objection is the strongest point against preemption, but it assumes away the central problem: LHEPA was applied as a merits-stage filter that effectively adds a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct element to federal ADA/§ 504 liability, which Howlett and Haywood forbid regardless of the ultimate remedy. Even accepting that Title III generally limits private plaintiffs to prospective relief and that Cummings narrows § 504 damages, those remedial constraints are Congress’s choices and do not authorize a State to alter the substantive duty (discrimination/reasonable modification) Congress enacted. Justice Barrett’s concern about advisory constitutional rulings would have more force if the federal claims were remediless, but prospective relief and fees remain at least plausible on this record, so LHEPA’s merits overlay can still nullify operative federal entitlements. The narrow textualist disposition is to reverse insofar as LHEPA was used to defeat the federal claims on the merits, while leaving the scope of permissible remedies under Title III and Cummings for remand, as Justice Kagan proposes.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest point that Howlett/Haywood generally forbid a State from using a heightened culpability overlay as a merits-stage gatekeeper to a federal claim, even where remedies are limited to prospective relief and fees. But Chief Justice Roberts persuasively identifies an antecedent vehicle problem: on this record petitioner has not shown that LHEPA actually foreclosed any concrete, otherwise-available federal relief, given Title III’s generally injunctive-only private enforcement and Cummings’s elimination of the emotional-distress damages theory driving the § 504 claim. Without a clear, outcome-determinative clash—particularly as to prospective relief or fees as applied—a broad Supremacy Clause ruling risks being unnecessary and close to advisory, contrary to my institutionalist preference for narrow decisions that preserve the Court’s legitimacy. I would therefore affirm on the remedial/record ground while reserving Howlett/Haywood’s full force for a cleaner case where a viable federal remedy is denied solely because a state immunity overlay rewrote federal liability.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the best point that Howlett and Haywood forbid a State from using a state-law “immunity” or heightened culpability requirement to rewrite the merits of a federal cause of action, even when the federal remedy is primarily injunctive or fees. But I agree with the Chief Justice that those cases still presuppose a concrete displacement of some federally available relief, and this record does not clearly show LHEPA was outcome-determinative as to prospective relief or fees, while the pleaded damages theory is largely unavailable under Title III and (after Cummings) under § 504. Under a textualist/originalist approach, I would not issue a Supremacy Clause holding in the abstract when we cannot identify an operative federal entitlement that the state rule actually nullified as applied here. If a cleaner vehicle shows a viable federal remedy denied solely because a State imposed an emergency-immunity merits filter, Howlett/Haywood would likely control and I would be prepared to find preemption then.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s remedial-threshold concern is the strongest point for respondent, but I do not think remedial uncertainty makes the Supremacy Clause conflict “abstract” when LHEPA is being used, as Justice Kagan explains, as a merits-stage filter that adds gross-negligence/willful-misconduct elements Congress did not enact. Howlett and Haywood—which Justice Sotomayor emphasizes—treat that kind of state-law redefinition of federal liability as preempted even before we sort out the ultimate menu of remedies, because it predictably suppresses forward-looking relief and attorney’s fees that remain available under Title III and (at least in some forms) § 504 even after Cummings. Justice Barrett’s worry about an advisory ruling is answered by a narrow disposition: reverse only to the extent the state court applied LHEPA to defeat federal liability, and remand for the lower courts to apply the federal remedial limits (including Cummings and Title III’s constraints) in the first instance. Under my pragmatic approach, allowing states to elevate culpability standards in emergency settings would systematically under-enforce disability protections where procedural fairness and practical consequences are most acute.

John Roberts.reasoning: On this record, the petition appears to seek damages relief that is independently unavailable under the asserted federal causes of action: Title III of the ADA generally authorizes only injunctive relief in private suits, and emotional-distress damages are unavailable under § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act after Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller. Given that threshold remedial defect, it is unnecessary to reach the broader Supremacy Clause question whether Louisiana’s LHEPA gross-negligence/willful-misconduct standard can modify the elements or liability standard of a federal disability-discrimination claim. Deciding preemption here would risk an unnecessarily sweeping ruling with significant federalism implications and uncertain factual predicates about how, precisely, the state courts applied LHEPA to the federal claims. If and when a case squarely presents a viable federal remedy yet is barred solely by a state immunity rule, Howlett v. Rose would provide the appropriate framework for assessing whether the state defense impermissibly defeats a federal cause of action.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Nothing in Title III of the ADA or § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act textually displaces a State’s general emergency-liability limitation for healthcare providers in its courts, and the Supremacy Clause preempts only where state law actually conflicts with federal law’s operative requirements. Unlike § 1983 in Haywood v. Drown and Howlett v. Rose—where States attempted to close their courts to a federal cause of action or confer immunity that would nullify a federally created remedy—the LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct standard does not, on this record, facially bar adjudication of an ADA/§ 504 claim as such and may operate as a generally applicable limit on damages liability during a declared emergency. In any event, petitioner’s theory seeks damages (notably emotional-distress damages) that are unavailable under § 504 after Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, and Title III private suits generally provide injunctive relief rather than compensatory damages, so the asserted federal “right” purportedly obstructed by LHEPA is not clearly established. Applying an original public meaning approach, absent a clear congressional command to override state emergency immunities, I would not infer preemption here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Whatever the outer limits of Howlett v. Rose’s rule that a State may not apply its own immunity law to defeat a federal cause of action in state court, petitioner faces a threshold remedial defect independent of LHEPA: Title III of the ADA does not authorize the compensatory damages he seeks, and under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller emotional-distress damages are unavailable under § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (a Spending Clause statute). Given that reality, applying LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct standard during a declared emergency does not meaningfully obstruct Congress’s remedial scheme here, because the federal statutes themselves sharply limit available private relief. Textually and as a practical matter, this looks less like a State nullifying federal rights and more like petitioner attempting to repackage a state-law medical-care grievance into federal civil-rights damages that Congress has not authorized.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Louisiana may not apply LHEPA’s COVID-era immunity (gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold) in state court in a way that effectively changes the elements or defeats liability for federal ADA Title III and Rehabilitation Act § 504 discrimination claims, because state-law immunities cannot be used to nullify or burden federal rights under the Supremacy Clause. Under Howlett v. Rose, a State that opens its courts to similar claims must hear federal causes of action on their federal terms and may not interpose state-law defenses that function as immunity from federal liability. Whatever limits exist on remedies for these federal statutes—e.g., Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller foreclosing emotional-distress damages under § 504—those are questions of federal remedial scope, not a license for States to add a heightened culpability requirement that obstructs Congress’s anti-discrimination mandate. Allowing emergency-triggered state immunity to dilute federal disability protections would predictably fall hardest on vulnerable patients who rely on equal access to care, undermining uniform enforcement of civil-rights guarantees.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under the Supremacy Clause, a state court may not apply a state-law immunity or heightened culpability requirement in a way that effectively defeats or redefines the elements of a federal cause of action; Howlett v. Rose makes clear that state-law defenses that are inconsistent with federal law must give way when a State entertains the federal claim. LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold operates as a substantive shield for defendants, not a neutral rule of court administration, and as applied here it risks displacing Congress’s chosen liability standard for discrimination under the ADA and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act. Respondents’ remedial arguments (including Cummings and limits on Title III damages) may narrow what relief is available, but they do not justify importing LHEPA to heighten the liability standard for the federal right itself. The workable middle ground is to hold LHEPA preempted to the extent it purports to alter federal ADA/RA liability while leaving state law free to regulate parallel state tort claims and leaving respondents to press any federal limits on remedies on remand.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause requires state courts to give federal causes of action the same substantive force they would have in federal court, and a State may not graft a state-law immunity or heightened culpability element (gross negligence/willful misconduct under LHEPA) onto Congress’s liability standards under Title III of the ADA and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act. Under Howlett v. Rose, a state-law defense that effectively defeats a federal right—because it is not a neutral rule of judicial administration but a substantive immunity—must yield when applied to a federal claim. Whatever limits federal law itself places on remedies (e.g., Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller restricting emotional-distress damages under § 504, and Title III’s remedial limits), those are questions of federal statutory meaning; they do not authorize Louisiana to redefine the elements or defenses of the federal discrimination claims via LHEPA. Because LHEPA operates here as an obstacle to uniform enforcement of federal disability-rights guarantees by conditioning liability on a more demanding state standard, it is preempted as applied to these federal claims.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Even assuming Louisiana’s LHEPA gross-negligence/willful-misconduct standard cannot be used to alter the substantive elements of federal ADA/§ 504 claims under the Supremacy Clause, petitioner still must show a viable federal remedy. Title III of the ADA generally provides injunctive relief rather than compensatory damages, and under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. (2022), emotional-distress damages are unavailable under Spending Clause statutes like § 504, substantially undercutting the petition’s practical stakes. Given that the petition appears to seek primarily damages that federal law does not authorize, and mindful of judicial restraint and avoiding broad constitutional rulings where the case can be resolved on narrower grounds, I would vote to affirm. Cases like Haywood v. Drown, 556 U.S. 729 (2009), and Williams v. Reed (2025) underscore that states may not nullify federal causes of action, but this record does not convincingly show LHEPA actually foreclosed otherwise-available federal relief here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: As a threshold matter, petitioner’s requested relief appears independently foreclosed because private Title III ADA actions do not authorize compensatory damages, and under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. (2022), emotional-distress damages are unavailable under § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act as a Spending Clause statute. Even assuming Louisiana’s LHEPA gross-negligence/willful-misconduct standard was applied to “heighten” the merits standard for federal discrimination claims, petitioner has not shown that doing so was outcome-determinative as to any federally available remedy, which undercuts the asserted Supremacy Clause injury. While Haywood v. Drown, 556 U.S. 729 (2009), forbids state rules that effectively nullify federal causes of action in state court, this record—given the limited remedies under the ADA/RA—does not establish that LHEPA operated as a categorical bar to any viable federal claim rather than, at most, limiting state-law liability during an emergency. Absent a demonstrated conflict with the federal statutes’ text and remedial scheme, I would not find preemption here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: A state may not, consistent with the Supremacy Clause, apply a state-law immunity rule in a way that functionally rewrites the elements or culpability standard of a federal civil-rights claim and thereby obstructs Congress’s chosen enforcement scheme. Under Haywood v. Drown and related preemption principles, Louisiana cannot condition adjudication of ADA Title III or Rehabilitation Act § 504 liability on showing “gross negligence or willful misconduct” where federal law imposes different substantive duties (e.g., reasonable modifications and nondiscrimination) and does not incorporate that heightened fault requirement. Respondents are correct that remedies limits (including Cummings’s bar on emotional-distress damages under § 504 and Title III’s remedial constraints) may narrow available relief, but a remedial shortfall does not justify importing LHEPA’s heightened culpability standard to defeat federal liability at the threshold. Procedural fairness and uniform federal rights counsel that state courts must hear and apply federal claims on their own terms rather than through state emergency-immunity overlays that impede meaningful enforcement.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Louisiana’s COVID-era health-emergency civil immunity statute (LHEPA) can be applied in state court to heighten the liability standard (gross negligence/willful misconduct) and thereby defeat federal disability-discrimination causes of action under Title III of the ADA and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Louisiana Health Emergency Powers Act (LHEPA) immunity provisions (as applied during the declared COVID-19 public health emergency) in interaction with Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. §§ 12181–12189) and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (29 U.S.C. § 794), including federal preemption/Supremacy Clause principles.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that his suit is a federal civil-rights action (ADA Title III and RA § 504), not a state tort claim, and that Louisiana courts impermissibly imported LHEPA’s heightened fault standard (gross negligence/willful misconduct) into the elements of federal claims, effectively conditioning and diluting federally created rights during an emergency. He contends this application creates an ‘absurd’ result because the alleged denial of aquatic therapy was unrelated to COVID-19 care, undermines uniform national enforcement of the ADA/RA, and is preempted under the Supremacy Clause because states may not use emergency immunity or state procedural devices to displace or narrow federal causes of action.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue the petition rests on an incorrect premise about remedies and fails on the merits because (1) the damages Petitioner seeks are unavailable in private enforcement—emotional distress damages are not recoverable under § 504 and Title III does not allow private-party damages—so even without LHEPA he could not obtain the compensatory relief he claims; and (2) the Louisiana courts properly applied LHEPA during the declared emergency to bar claims absent gross negligence or willful misconduct, with Petitioner’s allegations amounting at most to ordinary negligence. Respondents also emphasize that Petitioner’s preemption assertions were conclusory and unsupported in the lower courts, and that LHEPA contains no relevant limitation during the emergency that would make it preempted in this context.
key_precedents: Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. (2022) (no emotional distress damages under Spending Clause statutes such as Rehabilitation Act § 504)
Mills v. Hartford Healthcare Corp., 347 A.3d 605 (Conn. 2023) (state COVID immunity interpretation; nexus/connection discussion)
Resurgens, LLC v. Ervin, 894 S.E.2d 408 (Ga. 2023) (state COVID immunity interpretation)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are right about the governing principle in the abstract: under Howlett and Felder a State may not tack on an extra gross-negligence/willful-misconduct element that functions as a merits screen for ADA/§ 504 liability, and Haywood reinforces that States cannot selectively disable federal rights in their courts. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan stress, the problem here is application and consequence: this record does not clearly show LHEPA was actually used to redefine the federal elements (particularly as to prospective relief), rather than to limit damages exposure that federal law largely withholds under Title III and has narrowed under Cummings for § 504. Given that petitioner bears the burden to demonstrate a concrete conflict with Congress’s remedial design, I would resolve this case narrowly on the vehicle/remedies posture—affirming without announcing a broad reverse-Erie preemption rule for generally applicable emergency-liability statutes. That leaves open that a clearer case—where LHEPA unmistakably blocks federally authorized injunctive relief or is expressly treated as an additional element of federal liability—would be controlled by Howlett/Felder and could require preemption.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s vehicle/remedies point—that Title III is largely injunctive and Cummings narrows § 504 damages—does not answer the Supremacy Clause question identified by Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor: a State may not change the federal rule of decision by superadding a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct element to establish an ADA/§ 504 violation. Under Howlett and Felder, state-law “immunities” that function as merits screens are preempted regardless of how robust the particular remedy ultimately is, and Haywood confirms States cannot disable federal rights in their courts through state policy choices. Even accepting Justice Barrett’s caution about a thin record, the proper course is reversal and remand to apply the federal elements and defenses first, then restrict relief to what federal law authorizes, rather than allowing Louisiana to rewrite liability standards. The opposing side’s insistence on an outcome-determinative remedial clash misstates the original meaning of the Supremacy Clause’s command that federal law be supreme as law, not only when it yields substantial damages.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are right about the governing principle in the abstract: under Howlett and Felder a State may not add a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct element to the federal rule of decision. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett that petitioner has not carried the burden to show, on this record, that Louisiana applied LHEPA as a merits screen that actually displaced any federally available remedy (particularly prospective relief), rather than as a generally applicable emergency limitation bearing primarily on damages exposure that federal law largely does not authorize (Title III) or has sharply narrowed (Cummings under § 504). Haywood underscores the danger of state devices that selectively disable federal rights, yet that is precisely why I would not extend reverse-Erie/Supremacy Clause doctrine here without a clear, outcome-determinative conflict in application. If a future case cleanly showed LHEPA used to block federally authorized injunctive relief or otherwise redefine the federal elements, Howlett/Felder would control for me; this case does not present that showing.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s vehicle/remedies point is the strongest counter, but it misframes the conflict: under Howlett and Felder the Supremacy Clause injury occurs when a State adds a state-law culpability threshold to the federal rule of decision, regardless of whether damages are ultimately available in abundance. Justice Barrett’s distinction reinforces this—if LHEPA is functioning (as the state court’s approach suggests) as an “additional element” for ADA/§ 504 liability rather than a remedial cap, that is substantive displacement and nonuniform enforcement forbidden by Haywood. Even accepting Justice Kagan’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s prudential concern about generally applicable emergency statutes, federal civil-rights standards—at least for establishing a violation and obtaining federally authorized prospective relief—cannot turn on state emergency immunity without inviting forum-dependent dilution of protections for disabled people when they are most vulnerable. I would reverse narrowly to hold that Louisiana may not use LHEPA to alter what a plaintiff must prove to establish an ADA/§ 504 violation, leaving the scope of remedies (including Cummings’s limits) to federal-law analysis on remand.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are right on the governing principle: under Howlett and Felder, a State cannot add a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct element if it operates as a merits screen for ADA/§ 504 liability. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett that this case does not cleanly establish that Louisiana applied LHEPA that way as to any federally available remedy—especially prospective relief, which remains central under Title III and is not answered by petitioner’s damages-centered obstacle theory after Cummings. Haywood and Felder involved clear, outcome-altering devices aimed at disabling federal claims or access to a forum; here LHEPA looks facially general and the record ambiguity makes a broad reverse-Erie preemption holding imprudent on pragmatic textualist grounds. I would affirm narrowly, while making clear that if a future record shows LHEPA being used to bar federally authorized injunctive relief or to rewrite the federal elements, Howlett/Felder would likely control.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s vehicle/remedies point does not answer the core Supremacy Clause defect: under Howlett and Felder, a State may not rewrite the federal rule of decision by layering on a state-law gross-negligence/willful-misconduct screen for ADA/§ 504 liability, regardless of how robust the ultimate damages catalog is. Justice Barrett’s distinction between limiting a state-law damages theory and imposing a liability gatekeeper is exactly right, and—taking Justice Sotomayor’s premise seriously—the state court applied LHEPA as a merits filter for the federal claim itself. Haywood reinforces that States cannot manipulate enforcement of federal rights in their courts by interposing state-law obstacles, even if styled as generally applicable or emergency-driven. The proper disposition is narrow but clear: federal elements and defenses govern liability, and any remedy limitations should come from federal law, not from a state-created heightened-fault prerequisite.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are right on the general doctrinal proposition from Howlett and Felder: a State may not add a state-law immunity or heightened-fault element as a merits screen to a federal cause of action. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively show this is a flawed vehicle because petitioner has not demonstrated on this record that LHEPA actually displaced any federally authorized remedy, especially prospective relief that remains central under Title III, and Cummings significantly narrows the damages theories petitioner seems to rely on under § 504. Unlike Haywood/Felder, LHEPA appears generally applicable in an emergency context rather than a targeted, forum-manipulating obstacle, and institutional restraint counsels against issuing a broad reverse-Erie/Supremacy Clause ruling without a clear, outcome-determinative conflict. I would leave open that if LHEPA were shown to bar federally authorized injunctive relief or otherwise clearly alter the federal rule of decision as to available remedies, preemption would be warranted in a cleaner case.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are right on the doctrinal principle: under Howlett and Felder, a State cannot add a state-law immunity or heightened-fault element that functions as an additional merits screen for a federal cause of action, and Haywood reinforces that States may not disable federal rights in their courts. But Chief Justice Roberts’s vehicle point remains decisive for me as a textualist applying conflict/obstacle preemption: on this record, petitioner has not shown that LHEPA actually displaced any federally authorized remedy, given Title III’s generally prospective-only private relief and Cummings’s significant constraints on § 504 damages. Without a concrete showing that LHEPA barred federally available injunctive relief or otherwise altered the federal rule of decision as applied to an available remedy, I would not announce a broad reverse-Erie rule for a generally applicable emergency-liability statute. I would affirm narrowly, while leaving open that a cleaner case demonstrating outcome-determinative interference with federal elements or prospective relief would warrant preemption under Howlett/Felder.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s vehicle/remedies concern is the strongest point for Respondent, but it asks the wrong threshold question: whether meaningful damages remain, rather than whether Louisiana may alter the federal rule of decision by requiring gross negligence/willful misconduct to establish an ADA/§ 504 violation. Under Howlett and Felder (as Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch emphasize), a State cannot use a generally applicable immunity as a merits gatekeeper for federal claims in its courts; even if relief is primarily prospective, plaintiffs retain a federally conferred right to prove a violation and obtain whatever Congress authorizes without state-law dilution. Haywood reinforces that forum-dependent handicapping of federal rights is impermissible, and the nonuniformity problem is concrete even where the remedy ultimately proves limited. Pragmatically, allowing emergency-immunity policy to recast federal antidiscrimination standards predictably weakens procedural fairness and access for disabled people during crises, when uniform federal protections matter most.

John Roberts.reasoning: Even assuming the Supremacy Clause limits a State’s ability to interpose state-law immunities against federally created rights, this case is a poor vehicle to resolve that broad question because the remedies Petitioner seeks largely appear unavailable under federal law in any event: Title III of the ADA generally does not authorize private damages, and under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. (2022), emotional-distress damages are not recoverable under § 504. Against that remedial backdrop, Louisiana’s application of LHEPA’s heightened culpability standard during a declared emergency does not clearly “defeat” a viable federal damages claim, and I would avoid a sweeping preemption ruling that could unsettle state emergency-response frameworks absent a clear conflict. Howlett v. Rose, 496 U.S. 356 (1990), and Felder v. Casey, 487 U.S. 131 (1988), reserve serious limits on discriminatory or outcome-altering state rules, but here the record and posture do not require us to decide the outer boundary of those principles for ADA/RA claims. A narrow disposition affirming on the lack of available compensatory relief best respects precedent and institutional legitimacy while leaving the broader reverse-Erie/preemption issue for a cleaner case.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under the Supremacy Clause, a State may not apply a state-law immunity or heightened fault rule that effectively nullifies or discriminates against a federally created cause of action; the elements and standard of liability for Title III of the ADA (42 U.S.C. §§ 12181–12189) and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794) are matters of federal law. Applying LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold to these federal discrimination claims impermissibly alters the federal right and operates as a categorical bar in state court, contrary to this Court’s holding that States cannot withdraw jurisdiction or manipulate substantive standards to defeat federal civil-rights actions. Although Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. (2022), limits certain damages under § 504, that remedial limitation does not authorize a State to graft additional state-law immunity elements onto the federal cause of action itself. Accordingly, Louisiana’s application of LHEPA in this manner is preempted and cannot be used to defeat the federal ADA/RA claims.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Nothing in Title III of the ADA authorizes private-party damages, and after Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. (2022), emotional-distress damages are unavailable under Rehabilitation Act § 504, substantially undercutting Petitioner’s premise that LHEPA’s heightened fault standard "defeated" a meaningful federal damages remedy. Unlike the state-law obstacles in Felder v. Casey (state notice-of-claim regime) and Haywood v. Drown (jurisdiction-stripping/targeted immunity aimed at nullifying federal claims), LHEPA is a generally applicable emergency-liability rule tied to the State’s management of a declared public-health crisis and does not purport to rewrite the elements of ADA/§ 504 discrimination as such. Given the practical consequences in an emergency and the absence of a clear congressional directive displacing state emergency-liability protections in this setting, I would not extend reverse-Erie/Supremacy Clause doctrine to preempt LHEPA on this record. At minimum, Petitioner has not shown that applying LHEPA creates an impermissible obstacle to the federal remedial scheme where the relief sought is largely unavailable as a matter of federal law.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Louisiana may not, consistent with the Supremacy Clause, apply LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold to effectively rewrite the elements or liability standard of federal disability-discrimination claims under Title III of the ADA and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, because state-law immunity rules that “thwart the congressional remedy” are preempted. Felder v. Casey makes clear that a State cannot use an immunity or special restriction to narrow federally created rights in its own courts, and Brown v. Western Ry. of Ala. likewise rejects state rules that unduly burden federal causes of action and undermine uniform enforcement. Respondents are correct that Title III generally does not authorize private damages and Cummings bars emotional-distress damages under § 504, but those remedial limits do not permit a State to dilute federal liability standards where other federally authorized relief (including injunctive relief and potentially other forms of compensatory relief under § 504 where available) remains at stake. Given the real-world impact on disabled individuals’ access to medically necessary services, LHEPA cannot be used as a categorical, emergency-triggered barrier to federal antidiscrimination enforcement absent a clear congressional authorization.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title III of the ADA authorizes private plaintiffs to obtain injunctive relief, not compensatory damages, and after Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. (2022), emotional-distress damages are unavailable under § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, substantially undercutting Petitioner’s theory that LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct standard “defeated” a federal damages remedy. While the Supremacy Clause forbids States from burdening or nullifying federal causes of action in state court (Felder v. Casey, 487 U.S. 131 (1988)), this record reads less like a state procedural trap and more like a generally applicable emergency-liability limitation that does not alter the federal elements of discrimination so much as limit a category of state-law liability during a declared emergency. Given the limited private-remedy structure Congress chose for Title III and § 504, and absent a clearer showing that Louisiana’s rule operated as an obstacle to federally prescribed enforcement mechanisms (particularly prospective relief), I would not find preemption here. On these facts, the state court’s application of LHEPA does not appear to be the kind of discriminatory or uniquely burdensome rule condemned in Felder or Haywood.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under the Supremacy Clause, a State may not apply a state-law “no-liability” or immunity rule in its courts in a way that functionally nullifies a federally created cause of action or alters its substantive elements. Louisiana’s LHEPA gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold is a state tort-standard that cannot be imported to heighten the plaintiff’s burden on federal disability-discrimination claims under Title III of the ADA and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, whose elements Congress supplied. Haywood v. Drown makes clear that a State cannot evade federal law by closing its courthouse doors (or effectively doing so) to federal claims through a categorical immunity/jurisdictional device, and the same principle applies when the State recasts federal rights as subject to a heightened fault prerequisite. While Cummings limits available remedies under § 504 (and Title III limits private damages), remedy limits do not authorize States to redefine liability standards for federal rights; the proper course is to apply federal elements and then award only the remedies federal law allows.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioner’s requested relief largely does not fit the federal causes of action he invokes: Title III of the ADA generally provides only injunctive relief in private suits, and under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C. (2022), emotional-distress damages are unavailable under § 504, substantially undercutting the claim that LHEPA’s gross-negligence standard “defeats” a federal damages remedy. Given that remedial backdrop, applying Louisiana’s emergency immunity rule as a generally applicable limitation on civil liability during a declared public health emergency is not shown here to create the kind of direct obstacle to Congress’s enforcement scheme that triggers Supremacy Clause displacement. Unlike Felder v. Casey (1988) and Haywood v. Drown (2009), Louisiana has not imposed a special state-court-only procedural hurdle or closed its courts to federal claims; the core federal right to seek prospective relief remains, and judicial restraint counsels against broad preemption on a thin record. Practical workability and respect for state emergency measures, absent a clear conflict with federal law’s text or remedies, support affirmance.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under the Supremacy Clause, a State may not apply a state-law immunity or heightened-fault rule in a way that substantively defeats a federally created cause of action in state court, see Felder v. Casey and Howlett v. Rose; if Louisiana courts truly imported LHEPA’s “gross negligence/willful misconduct” standard as an additional element of ADA Title III or Rehabilitation Act § 504 liability, that application would be preempted. But the petitioner’s requested relief appears largely unavailable as a matter of federal law: Title III does not authorize private-party damages and, under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, emotional-distress damages are not recoverable under § 504, which substantially undermines any showing that LHEPA’s standard “defeated” a viable federal remedy. On this record, and given the absence of a clearly preserved, developed preemption theory demonstrating that LHEPA operated as a discriminatory “condition” on federal rights (rather than a generally applicable state limitation relevant only to state-law damages claims), I would affirm. Methodological consistency counsels deciding the case on the federal statutes’ remedial limits rather than extending reverse-Erie preemption without a clear conflict.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Louisiana may not use LHEPA’s emergency immunity to alter the substantive elements or available enforcement of federal disability-discrimination causes of action, because under the Supremacy Clause state-law defenses that are not applicable to analogous federal claims—or that effectively nullify them—are preempted. Howlett v. Rose holds that a State cannot apply state-law immunities in its courts to defeat a federally created cause of action, and importing a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold into ADA Title III and Rehabilitation Act § 504 claims risks exactly that kind of displacement. Even acknowledging limits on remedies (e.g., Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller foreclosing emotional-distress damages under § 504, and Title III’s general unavailability of private damages), plaintiffs retain federal rights to prove statutory violations and obtain appropriate relief, and a state emergency statute cannot condition those rights on heightened fault. As a matter of procedural fairness and practical consequences, permitting LHEPA to dilute federal civil-rights enforcement would produce nonuniform access to federal protections depending on the forum and the breadth of a State’s emergency immunity regime.
